name: Alexandria
info: Alexandria is a port city on Egypt's Mediterranean coast, at the western edge of the Nile Delta. Alexander the Great founded it in 331 BCE, and it became a Ptolemaic capital, a centre of learning and Egypt's chief seaport.

facts.founded: April 331 BCE by Alexander the Great (the exact date is disputed), on the site of an Egyptian village called Rhakotis; the architect was Dinocrates of Rhodes
facts.where: On the southern shore of the Mediterranean at the western edge of the Nile Delta, between the sea and Lake Mareotis, in northern Egypt
facts.known: The Lighthouse of Alexandria (the Pharos); the Library and Museion; the Ptolemaic court; the Septuagint; the Patriarchate of Alexandria; the Serapeum; the medieval spice trade; the bombardment of 1882
facts.today: Alexandria is the second largest city of Egypt after Cairo and its principal seaport.

t: Alexander founded the city in 331 BCE and the Ptolemies, who ruled Egypt from it from 305 BCE, made it the largest city in the world within about a century, with a Library and Museion and the Pharos lighthouse.
Under Rome it remained a granary and a centre of Christian theology, but suffered riots, a massacre under Caracalla, a tsunami in 365 CE and the destruction of the Serapeum in 391.
After the Arab conquest of 641 the capital moved to Fustat; the city declined under the Ottomans and revived from about 1810 under Muhammad Ali, until the bombardment of 1882.
dyk: The Lighthouse of Alexandria, reputed to be 138 metres high, was begun by Ptolemy I and finished under Ptolemy II at a cost of 800 talents. Earthquakes destroyed it in the 14th century, and the Qaitbay citadel of 1477 stands on its site.
ev: Alexander the Great founds the city
Ptolemy declares himself Pharaoh and moves his capital from Memphis to Alexandria
Julius Caesar is besieged in the city, and the Library faces destruction
Theodosius I orders the destruction of pagan temples and the Serapeum is destroyed
The Arabs under Amr ibn al-As take the city after a siege of fourteen months
Crusaders led by Peter of Cyprus take and sack the city
French troops storm the city during Napoleon's expedition
British naval forces bombard and occupy the city

sections.origins:
Radiocarbon dating of seashell fragments and lead contamination show human activity at the site during the Old Kingdom and again from 1000 to 800 BCE. Ancient sources mention a trading post here in the time of Rameses the Great, trading with Crete, but it had long been lost by Alexander's arrival. A small Egyptian fishing village, Rhakotis, existed in the vicinity from the 13th century BCE and became the Egyptian quarter of the city. To the east, where Abu Qir Bay now lies, the port cities of Canopus and Heracleion existed from the 7th century BCE; Heracleion was rediscovered underwater in recent years.

Alexander founded the city in April 331 BCE, though the exact date is disputed, after capturing Egypt from the Persians. He wanted a large Greek city on the coast that would bear his name, and chose a site behind the island of Pharos, to be joined to the shore by a causeway so as to make two harbours. It was meant to supersede the older Greek colony of Naucratis and to link Greece with the Nile valley. The ancient accounts are numerous and varied. Arrian gives one of the more sober, in which Alexander, lacking chalk, marked out the plan with grain; more fanciful myths are in the Alexander Romance. A few months later Alexander left Egypt and never returned. His viceroy Cleomenes continued the work, and Dinocrates of Rhodes designed the city on a grid plan.
sections.growth:
After Alexander's death in 323 BCE his general Ptolemy took Egypt and brought the body to Egypt. He first ruled from Memphis; in 305 BCE he declared himself Pharaoh as Ptolemy I Soter and moved the capital to Alexandria. Inheriting the trade of ruined Tyre and becoming the centre of new commerce between Europe and the Arabian and Indian East, the city grew within a generation to be larger than Carthage. In a century it was the largest city in the world and for some centuries after, second only to Rome. The Heptastadion, a causeway of 1,260 metres joining Pharos to the mainland, and the Lighthouse followed under Ptolemy I, with the Serapeum; the Museion was built under Ptolemy II and the Ptolemaic mausolea under Ptolemy IV.

A census of 32 CE counted over 180,000 adult male citizens, besides freedmen, women, children and slaves. Estimates of the total population range from 216,000 to 500,000, and some give 500,000 to 600,000 under the Roman principate. In the late medieval period Alexandria again became Egypt's most important commercial port. Goods from Arabia, India, South-East Asia and Africa came by the Red Sea, the port of Aydhab and the Nile, and Venetians, Genoese, Pisans and Catalans kept funduqs, fortified quarters under a consul, there. After the Portuguese sea route to India of 1498 its trade declined. The Mahmoudiyah Canal, built in 1820, restored its prominence, and by 1850 the city had returned to something like its former glory.
sections.rulers:
Alexander's viceroy Cleomenes ruled the new city until Ptolemy had him executed in 322 or 321 BCE. From 305 BCE the Ptolemies ruled Egypt from Alexandria. Rome had influence for over a hundred years before the will of Ptolemy Alexander placed the city formally under Roman jurisdiction in 80 BCE. Julius Caesar was in Alexandria in 47 BCE, courting Cleopatra and besieged by her brother and rival. Mark Antony followed his example, and after Antony's defeat at Actium Octavian took Egypt as the emperor's personal property, appointing a prefect who answered to him and not to the Senate. The city commanded an important granary of Rome, one of the reasons he placed it under imperial power.

The Persian king Khosrau II took the city in 619, and the Byzantine emperor Heraclius recovered it a few years later. In 641 the Arabs under Amr ibn al-As took it after a siege of fourteen months; the Byzantines held it again for a time from 645, but it fell for good in 646, ending 975 years of Greco-Roman control. A new capital, Fustat, was founded on the Nile. Between 814 and 827 Andalusian pirates held the city. It was part of the Ayyubid and Mamluk states, passed to the Ottomans after the Battle of Ridaniya in 1517, and stayed Ottoman until 1798. The French held it until 1801, when the British took it. Muhammad Ali, the Ottoman governor of Egypt, began its rebuilding around 1810. After the British occupation that began in 1882, the army in the coup of 1952 occupied Alexandria and drove King Farouk from Montaza Palace.
sections.life:
The early Ptolemies kept apart the three largest groups of the population, Greek, Jewish and Egyptian. At first Egyptians were probably the plurality. Law was based on Greek, especially Attic, law, and non-Greek texts entered the Library only once translated into Greek. The city had the largest Jewish community of the ancient world, and the Septuagint, a Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible, was produced there. The ancient city had a Greek royal quarter called the Brucheum, the Egyptian Rhakotis and a Jewish quarter in the northeast; two colonnaded main streets, said to be about 60 metres wide, crossed near the Soma, Alexander's mausoleum.

The Ptolemies fostered the Library and the Museion into a centre of Hellenistic learning. Euclid, Hipparchus and Eratosthenes, who became head librarian and calculated the Earth's circumference, are associated with the Museion. Strabo listed Alexandria with Tarsus and Athens among the learned cities. Alexandria later became a centre of Christian theology and church government: Arianism came to prominence there, and Athanasius opposed it. In the Islamic period Ibn Battuta wrote of Muslim saints living in the city. In the 19th century Greeks, then other Europeans, moved in. The poet Constantine Cavafy was born there, and E. M. Forster (in the First World War) and Lawrence Durrell (in the Second) worked in the city and wrote about it.
sections.crises:
According to one account the Library faced destruction during Caesar's siege of 47 BCE. According to another, the Serapeum of the Great Library was destroyed in 391, after Theodosius I ordered the destruction of pagan temples and Patriarch Theophilus complied, possibly ending the Library; libraries were closed in the same persecution of pagans. A persistent belief holds that the Library and its contents were destroyed in 642 in the Arab invasion. Which of these ended the Library is not settled. The neoplatonist philosopher Hypatia was publicly murdered by a Christian mob in this period.

Philo reports that in 38 CE disturbances between Jews and Greeks began during a visit by Agrippa I and led to violence and the desecration of synagogues. Riots followed in 66, and large parts of the city were destroyed in the revolt of 115. In 215 Caracalla ordered his troops to kill all youths able to bear arms, after satires against him; according to Cassius Dio over 20,000 people were killed. On 21 July 365 a tsunami from an earthquake near Crete devastated the city. Earthquakes struck in 956, 1303 and 1323, and destroyed the Lighthouse in the 14th century. In 1365 Crusaders under Peter of Cyprus took the city and sacked it brutally. The bombardment of July 1882 was the first battle of the Anglo-Egyptian War, and large sections were damaged or burned in the fires that followed.
sections.legacy:
Alexander's tomb, closed to the public in the 3rd century CE, has been forgotten; Greek excavators looked for it without success. Two obelisks known as Cleopatra's Needles stood by the Caesareum, and were taken to New York and London. Pompey's Pillar, a Roman column, 30 metres high with its pedestal, still stands. The catacombs of Kom El Shoqafa were found by accident in 1900, and Kom El Deka has revealed a theatre and Roman baths. The modern city stands over the ancient one, so excavation is difficult; since 1992 Franck Goddio's team has explored the sunken palace quarter and the island of Antirhodos, drowned by earthquakes and tsunamis. The Citadel of Qaitbay was built in 1477 on the site of the Lighthouse. The Coptic Orthodox Church and the Greek Orthodox Church of Alexandria both claim the ancient Patriarchate.

Britain kept the city within its sphere of influence for 150 years. In July 1954 it was bombed in what became known as the Lavon Affair, and on 26 October 1954 an attempt was made on Nasser's life in Mansheya Square. After the Suez Crisis of 1956 Europeans began to leave, and nationalisations to 1961 drove out nearly all the rest. Alexandria is now Egypt's second largest city and principal seaport. It has more than five million people, counted over an area wider than the municipal limits.

summary: Alexander the Great founded Alexandria in 331 BCE, and as the Ptolemaic capital it became the largest city in the world, with a Library and the Pharos lighthouse. It lost the capital to Fustat after the Arab conquest, declined, and was rebuilt from about 1810.
references: Islam Issa, Alexandria: The City That Changed the World (Pegasus Books, 2024)
notes: The Library: the city article says only that the Library 'faced destruction during Caesar's siege of Alexandria in 47 BC'; the history article says the Serapeum 'was destroyed, possibly effecting the final destruction of the Library' in 391, and that there is 'a persistent belief' it was destroyed in 642. Neither article describes the Library's holdings, size or a Caesar fire. I attributed each and did not choose. The articles give no 'legend' account of the Library beyond the 642 belief.

The Pharos: both articles give 138 m as 'reputed'; the city article gives 800 talents and 12 years and says Ptolemy I began it and Ptolemy II finished it. The history article puts the Lighthouse under Ptolemy I and 'followed soon after' the Heptastadion. The city article says destroyed by an earthquake in the 14th century; Ibn Battuta found it partly ruined in 1326 and impossible to enter by 1349 (not used: only 'destroyed in the 14th century'). The Qaitbay citadel date 1477 is from the city article.
Foundation date: the history article says 331 BC with the exact date disputed; the city article says April 331 BC. I used 331 BCE and noted the dispute.

Heraclius: the city article gives 629; the history article 'a few years later' after 619. I used 629 with the other's wording noted. The Arab siege (14 months) and 641 agree. The history article adds the 645 recapture and the fall in 646, and '975 years of Greco-Roman control'.

Quarters: the city article lists three regions (Rhakotis, Brucheum, Jewish quarter) and four in Roman times; the history article says the Jews occupied two of the five quarters. I used the city article's layout only and left out 'two of five'.

Population: 180,000 adult male citizens by a census of 32 CE; estimates of the total 216,000 to 500,000 (city article, under the 1st century); but the city article's History says 500,000 to 600,000 under the Roman principate, which sits oddly beside the 216,000 to 500,000 range. Both given, unreconciled. 1798 French estimates of 8,000 and 15,000 and the 'small fishing village' of the late Ottoman period are in the history article; not used (the history article also says 'by 1700 a small town amid ruins').

Medieval importance: the history article says Alexandria declined after Fustat became capital and 'emerged as a major metropolis' in the late medieval period, and that it was sacked in 1365 and declined after 1498; the city article says it lost importance to Rosetta 'during the 9th to 18th centuries', which overlaps the metropolis period. I did not state a Rosetta period. The history article says the city lost its Nile water supply under the Ottomans; the Mahmoudiyah Canal date (1820) is from the city article only.

Left out as unreliable or off-topic: climate change and sea-level figures, transport, education, culture, sport, mayors, notable people, the 2018 and 2022 finds, the Ayyubid 'emirate' note about Turan Shah, the 828 theft of Mark's body (Venetian merchants), Andalusian pirates only briefly. 'Cleopatra's Needles' taken to New York and London is in the city article.
Present day: the city article gives 5,700,000 for 2024 for an agglomeration over 1,661 km2 that extends beyond the municipal limits; I said so.

Wanted but not found: Ptolemy dates of the Library's founding; the Library's size; the Arab conquest's effect on the city's population; any date for the Alexandrian Jewish revolt's end; population in the 19th century after 1798; anything on the 1882 bombardment's casualties or cause.
